Microbe & Inf.: HPAI Virus H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in Wild Rats in Egypt during 2023 CDC MMWR: HPAI H5N1 Virus Infection of Indoor Domestic Cats Within Dairy Industry Worker Households — Michigan, May 2024 The USDA's Detections of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Mammals dashboard lists more than 200 feline detections in the U.S. and a dozen H5N1 positive rats. Curiously, while I can find one entry of a cat from Bond County Illinois in March of 2025 (which may, or may not, refer to the cat in this study), there appear to be no reports of any rats infected in Illinois. According to this report, a farmer brought the remains of six animals (a chicken, a turkey, a goose, 2 Guinea fowl, and a rat (Rattus norvegicus)) to his veterinarian after nearly all of his chickens died. Suspecting H5N1, the vet sent the remains to the University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Diagnostic Laboratory (VMDL; Columbia, MO, USA) for postmortem examination. VMDL ran a qRT-PCR on 1 chicken sample, which came back presumptive positive for H5, and forwarded tissue samples to NVSL in Ames, IA for confirmatory testing (which verified HPAIV H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b virus). Four days after the first report, the local vet visited the farm and collected the remains of a 13-year-old cat and a second feral rat from the farm. They were then sent to the University of Illinois Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory (VDL) for necropsy and additional testing. According to this report, state and local authorities were notified, and the Illinois Department of Agriculture and USDA quarantined the farm and monitored it for 4 months. Today's report is primarily an analysis of the extensive infection of both the cat and the rat submitted to VDL. Sadly, while the first rat underwent necropsy, it was never tested for H5N1, so all we have…

papers.title: Antigenic and Molecular Genetic Evolution of Influenza Viruses in Kazakhstan from 2017 to 2025
papers.abstract: Influenza viruses undergo continuous genetic and antigenic evolution, making sustained surveillance essential for monitoring changes in virus circulation and vaccine relevance. We analyzed influenza epidemiology and viral evolution in Kazakhstan across eight consecutive epidemic seasons (2017/18–2024/25) using data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, together with antigenic characterization, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis. Influenza activity was almost undetectable during the 2020/21 season, followed by the re-emergence of A(H3N2)-dominated circulation in 2021/22. In 2022/23, influenza B predominated initially, followed by A(H1N1)pdm09, whereas A(H3N2) predominated in 2023/24. A total of 199 A(H1N1)pdm09, 157 A(H3N2), 105 B/Victoria, and 16 B/Yamagata viruses were genetically characterized. A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses showed successive replacement of 6B-derived lineages, with descendants of 6B.1A.5a.2a predominating in the post-pandemic period. A(H3N2) viruses showed substantial genetic diversification, progressing from 3C.2a descendants to 3C.2a1b-related viruses and subsequently to 2a.3a.1/J.2 viruses. Among B/Victoria viruses, V1A was successively replaced by V1A.3 and V1A.3a.2, with V1A.3a.2 accounting for 100% of genetically characterized viruses in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Antigenic analysis showed 16- to 32-fold lower HI titers for A(H1N1)pdm09 6B.1A.5a.2 viruses when tested against antisera to earlier vaccine/reference strains, whereas no detectable antigenic differences were observed between 6B.1A.5a.2a and its recent descendants. These findings demonstrate substantial post-pandemic changes in influenza epidemic timing, subtype dominance, and genetic composition in Kazakhstan, while circulating viruses remained within globally recognized evolutionary lineages. Integrated epidemiological, genetic, and antigenic surveillance is important for detecting emerging variants, assessing vaccine relevance, and supporting timely influenza prevention and control measures.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the antigenic and molecular genetic evolution of seasonal influenza viruses in Kazakhstan from 2017 to 2025. It highlights the dynamic changes in influenza subtype dominance and genetic composition over time, emphasizing the need for sustained surveillance to monitor vaccine relevance and guide prevention strategies. The research utilized data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, combined with antigenic characterization, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis. Key results include the successive replacement of 6B-derived lineages in A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses and substantial genetic diversification in A(H3N2) viruses. The study found that B/Victoria viruses were replaced by V1A.3a.2 in later seasons. These findings demonstrate the importance of integrated surveillance for tracking influenza evolution and supporting public health interventions. papers.title_zh: 2017年至2025年哈萨克斯坦流感病毒的抗原性和分子遗传 进化
papers.source_body_en: Influenza viruses undergo continuous genetic and antigenic evolution, making sustained surveillance essential for monitoring changes in virus circulation and vaccine relevance. We analyzed influenza epidemiology and viral evolution in Kazakhstan across eight consecutive epidemic seasons (2017/18–2024/25) using data from the national influenza sentinel surveillance system, together with antigenic characterization, Sanger sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, and phylogenetic analysis. Influenza activity was almost undetectable during the 2020/21 season, followed by the re-emergence of A(H3N2)-dominated circulation in 2021/22. In 2022/23, influenza B predominated initially, followed by A(H1N1)pdm09, whereas A(H3N2) predominated in 2023/24. A total of 199 A(H1N1)pdm09, 157 A(H3N2), 105 B/Victoria, and 16 B/Yamagata viruses were genetically characterized. A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses showed successive replacement of 6B-derived lineages, with descendants of 6B.1A.5a.2a predominating in the post-pandemic period. A(H3N2) viruses showed substantial genetic diversification, progressing from 3C.2a descendants to 3C.2a1b-related viruses and subsequently to 2a.3a.1/J.2 viruses. Among B/Victoria viruses, V1A was successively replaced by V1A.3 and V1A.3a.2, with V1A.3a.2 accounting for 100% of genetically characterized viruses in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Antigenic analysis showed 16- to 32-fold lower HI titers for A(H1N1)pdm09 6B.1A.5a.2 viruses when tested against antisera to earlier vaccine/reference strains, whereas no detectable antigenic differences were observed between 6B.1A.5a.2a and its recent descendants. These findings demonstrate substantial post-pandemic changes in influenza epidemic timing, subtype dominance, and genetic composition in Kazakhstan, while circulating viruses remained within globally recognized evolutionary lineages. Integrated epidemiological, genetic, and antigenic surveillance is important for detecting emerging variants, assessing vaccine relevance, and supporting timely influenza prevention and control measures.

news.content: Skip directly to site content Skip directly to search Skip directly to On This Page An official website of the United States government Here's how you know Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( ) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. FluView Explore This Topic Search Search Clear Search For Everyone Current Week: U.S. Influenza Surveillance Report U.S. Influenza Surveillance: Purpose and Methods View all search clear search FluView Menu clear search For Everyone Current Week: U.S. Influenza Surveillance Report U.S. Influenza Surveillance: Purpose and Methods View All Home Current Week: U.S. Influenza Surveillance Report U.S. Influenza Surveillance: Purpose and Methods View Menu Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report: Key Updates for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026 For Everyone Sept. 18, 2026, visit link for details. Key points Seasonal influenza activity is low. U.S. virologic surveillance Clinical Laboratories Nationally, during Week 35, the percentage of respiratory specimens testing positive for influenza virus in clinical laboratories was 1.3%. The results of tests performed by clinical laboratories nationwide are summarized below. Data from clinical laboratories (the percentage of specimens tested that are positive for influenza) are used to monitor whether influenza activity is increasing or decreasing. Results of tests from Clinical Laboratories Week 35 Data Cumulative since September 28, 2025 (Week 40) No. of specimens tested 26,520 3,025,072 No. of positive specimens (%) 348 (1.3%) 324,183 (10.7%) Positive specimens by type Influenza A 326 (93.7%) 228,380 (70.4%) Influenza B 22 (6.3%) 95,803 (29.6%) View Larger Influenza Positive Tests Reported to CDC by Clinical Laboratories, National Summary, 2025-26 Season, week ending Sep. 5, 2026 View Chart Data Public Health Laboratories The results of tests performed by public health laboratories nationwide are summarized below. Data from public health laboratories are used to monitor the proportion of circulating viruses that belong to each influenza virus type/subtype/lineage. Viruses known to be associated with recent live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) receipt or found upon further testing to be a vaccine virus are not included as they are not circulating influenza viruses. Results of tests from Public Health Laboratories Week 35 Data Cumulative since September 28, 2025 (Week 40) No. of specimens tested 334 108,219 No. of positive specimens 48 67,584 Positive specimens by type/subtype Influenza A 45 (93.8%) 56,575 (83.7%) Subtyping Performed 29 (64.4%) 46,464 (82.1%) (H1N1)pdm09 25 (86.2%) 6,680 (14.4%) H3N2 4 (13.8%) 39,782 (85.6%) H3N2v† 0 0 H5* 0 2 (<0.1%) Subtyping not performed 16 (35.6%) 10,111 (17.9%) Influenza B 3 (6.3%) 11,009 (16.3%) Lineage testing performed 1 (33.3%) 4,467 (40.6%) Yamagata lineage 0 0 Victoria lineage 1 (100%) 4,467 (100%) Lineage not performed 2 (66.7%) 6,542 (59.4%) *These data reflect specimens tested, and the number determined to be positive for influenza viruses at the public health labs (specimens tested are not the same as cases). The data does not reflect specimens tested only at CDC and could include more than one specimen tested per person. For more information on the number of people infected with A(H5) viruses, please visit the "How CDC is monitoring influenza data among people to better understand the current avian influenza A (H5N1) situation" †When an influenza virus that normally circulates in swine (but not people) is detected in a person, it is called a "variant" influenza virus. Most human infections with variant influenza viruses occur following exposure to swine, but person-to-person transmission can occur. It is important to note that in most cases, variant influenza viruses have not shown the ability to spread easily and sustainably from person to person. View Larger This graph reflects the number of specimens tested and the number determined to be positive for influenza viruses at the public health lab (specimens tested is not the same as cases). It does not reflect specimens tested only at CDC and could include... Show More View Chart Data Additional virologic surveillance information for current and past seasons: Surveillance Methods | FluView Interactive: National, Regional, and State Data or Age Data Novel Influenza A Virus Infections No new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported to CDC this week. The CSTE position statement, which includes updated case definitions for confirmed, probable, and suspected cases is available at http://www.cste.org/resource/resmgr/position_statements_files_2023/24-ID-09_Novel_Influenza_A.pdf. An up-to-date summary of confirmed novel influenza virus cases is available at https://gis.cdc.gov/grasp/fluview/Novel_Influenza.html. An up-to-date summary of human cases of avian influenza A(H5) virus by state and exposure source is available at www.cdc.gov/bird-flu/situation-summary/index.html. Information about avian influenza is available at https://www.cdc.gov/flu/avianflu/index.htm. analysis.time: The report covers Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, and was published on September 18, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The surveillance report is for the United States, focusing on national and regional data.
analysis.event: The report indicates that seasonal influenza activity is low during Week 35, ending September 5, 2026. It also notes no new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: During Week 35, 1.3% of respiratory specimens tested in clinical laboratories were positive for influenza virus. Influenza A accounted for 93.7% of positive specimens, while Influenza B accounted for 6.3%. No significant risk of widespread transmission was reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is monitoring influenza data through virologic surveillance and is providing interim recommendations for avian influenza A(H5N1) prevention and public health investigations. The data does not reflect specimens tested only at CDC and could include more than one specimen per person.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC's Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, indicates low seasonal influenza activity. During this period, 1.3% of respiratory specimens tested in clinical laboratories were positive for influenza, with Influenza A accounting for 93.7% and Influenza B for 6.3%. No new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported. The report emphasizes that variant influenza viruses, such as H5N1, have not shown the ability to spread easily and sustainably from person to person. The CDC is monitoring influenza data through virologic surveillance and has issued interim recommendations for avian influenza A(H5N1) prevention and public health investigations. The data reflects specimens tested at public health laboratories and may include multiple specimens per person. The report serves as a key update for understanding influenza trends and is part of broader surveillance efforts that include other respiratory viruses.
analysis.summary_en: The CDC's Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, indicates low seasonal influenza activity. news.title_zh: 美国每周流感监测报告:2026年9月5日当周第35周关键更新 - 美国疾病控制与预防中心 | CDC (.gov)
news.source_body_en: The CDC's Weekly US Influenza Surveillance Report for Week 35, ending September 5, 2026, indicates low seasonal influenza activity. During this period, 1.3% of respiratory specimens tested in clinical laboratories were positive for influenza, with Influenza A accounting for 93.7% and Influenza B for 6.3%. No new confirmed human infections with a novel influenza virus were reported. The report emphasizes that variant influenza viruses, such as H5N1, have not shown the ability to spread easily and sustainably from person to person. The CDC is monitoring influenza data through virologic surveillance and has issued interim recommendations for avian influenza A(H5N1) prevention and public health investigations. The data reflects specimens tested at public health laboratories and may include multiple specimens per person. The report serves as a key update for understanding influenza trends and is part of broader surveillance efforts that include other respiratory viruses.
news.content_zh: 美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)发布的2026年9月5日当周第35周美国流感监测报告指出,流感活动水平较低。在这一时期,临床实验室检测的呼吸道标本中有1.3%呈流感病毒阳性,其中甲型流感占93.7%,乙型流感占6.3%。未报告新的新型流感病毒人类感染病例。报告强调,H5N1等流感病毒变种尚未显示出在人与人之间容易且持续传播的能力。CDC通过病毒学监测监测流感数据,并发布了禽流感A(H5N1)预防和公共卫生调查的临时建议。这些数据反映了公共卫生实验室检测的标本,可能包含每人多个标本。该报告是了解流感趋势的关键更新,是更广泛监测工作的一部分,包括其他呼吸道病毒。

Publications/ Overview/ Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 595 Global Respiratory Virus Activity: Weekly Update N° 595 Week 36, ending 06 September 2026 16 September 2026 | Emergency situation update Download (5.8 MB) Overview In week 36 2026, globally, influenza positivity was around 10% and SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low. Influenza positivity was at 10% in the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas and tropical areas. Influenza positivity increased to 10% in the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas but there was also a decrease in the reported specimens tested for week 36. RSV positivity also remained low globally. Influenza Globally, influenza detections remained low in week 36 with influenza A viruses detections predominant. In the southern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Temperate South America and in single countries in Tropical South America and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in one country in Oceania where a small increase in activity was observed. A small increase in activity was also reported in a single country in Temperate South America. In the northern hemisphere, influenza percent positivity was elevated (>10%) in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa, Western, Southern, South-East and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in Tropical South America and Middle and Eastern Africa. Percent positivity was over 30% in some countries in Western Africa and Southern Asia and in a single country in South-East Asia. Increases in activity were observed in some countries in Western, Southern and South-East Asia and in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Northern Europe, Western and Eastern Africa, and Eastern Asia. In the zones with elevated positivity, influenza A(H3N2) was predominant in Western Africa, Eastern Asia and Oceania; influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 was predominant in Eastern Africa, Western, Southern and South-East Asia and influenza B was predominant in Temperate South America. Influenza A and B were codominant in Central America and the Caribbean and Tropical South America. SARS-CoV-2 Globally, SARS-CoV-2 positivity remained stable and low across most reporting countries, with elevated positivity (>10%) reported in some countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Northern and South West Europe and Eastern Asia, and in single countries in Tropical South America and Western, Southern and Eastern Asia. Small increases in activity were observed in countries in Northern Europe, and in single countries in Tropical South America, South West Europe and Western, South-East and Eastern Asia. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) RSV positivity was elevated (>10%) in a few countries in Central America and the Caribbean and Temperate South America and in single countries in Western Africa and Southern Asia. Percent positivity was over 30% in a single country in Temperate South America. Increases in activity were observed in single countries in Central America and the Caribbean, Western Africa and Southern Asia. RSV and influenza activity were both elevated in countries in Temperate South America, Western Africa and Southern Asia. Severity assessment The severity assessments here are reported from countries, areas and territories. Assessments for transmissibility can be reported based on syndromic parameters and/or influenza-specific parameters. In the southern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as low in a single country; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country. In the northern hemisphere temperate and subtropical areas, influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in 14 countries, and low and moderate in single countries; transmissibility using syndromic data was reported as below seasonal threshold in nine countries. Influenza-specific transmissibility was reported as below seasonal threshold in a single country in the tropical areas. WHO encourages countries, especially those that have received the multiplex influenza and SARS-CoV-2 reagent kits from GISRS, to conduct integrated surveillance of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 and report epidemiological and laboratory information in a timely manner to established regional and global platforms. The guidance can be found here. Starting with report #501, the Global Respiratory Virus Activity Weekly Update included data from sentinel surveillance and other types of systematically conducted virologic surveillance. Countries, areas, and territories use a variety of approaches to monitor respiratory virus activity and data in this report may vary from surveillance reports posted elsewhere. Analyses stratified by source of surveillance is available through Respimart. Among hospitalized children and adolescents, seasonal influenza is associated with greater clinical burden than COVID-19, including higher rates of intensive care unit (ICU) admission, complications, and antibiotic use, according to study findings published in The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. While COVID-19 and influenza generally cause mild illness in children, both infections can result in severe disease requiring hospitalization. Previous pediatric comparisons have produced varying results regarding the relative severity of these infections. Researchers conducted a nationwide prospective surveillance study to characterize differences in epidemiology, clinical presentation, disease severity, and outcomes between children hospitalized with COVID-19 and those hospitalized with influenza. Continued surveillance remains important to monitor changes in the clinical impact of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza in children and to inform vaccination and public health policy. The analysis included patients younger than 18 years hospitalized for more than 24 hours in Switzerland with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 or influenza infection between December 2018 and November 2023. COVID-19 cases were evaluated across periods dominated by wild-type SARS-CoV-2 (T1), Alpha (T2), Delta (T3), and Omicron (T4), while influenza cases were divided into pre-COVID and COVID-era periods. Among 4662 children included in the study, 3132 (67.2%) had SARS-CoV-2 infection and 1530 (32.8%) had influenza. Overall, 45.7% were girls, and more than half were 2 years of age or younger. Age patterns differed significantly by infection and study period (P <.001). Infants represented 32.2% to 46.7% of SARS-CoV-2 admissions across variant periods, whereas influenza admissions more frequently involved toddlers and school-aged children. At least 1 underlying condition was documented in 25.8% of the overall population, with prematurity and neurologic or neuromuscular conditions among the most common. Fever, cough, and rhinitis were common with both infections. The prevalence of fever among children with SARS-CoV-2 declined to 47.3% during the Omicron period, compared with 62.8%, 55.7%, and 64.9% during the wild-type, Alpha, and Delta periods, respectively. Fever occurred in 26.0% of influenza cases during the COVID-era period. Anosmia was limited to SARS-CoV-2 cases and occurred most frequently during the wild-type period (1.2%; P <.001). The researchers reported respiratory distress in 18.1% of children with influenza and 12.6% of those hospitalized during the Omicron period (P =.02). Overall, ICU admission occurred more frequently among children with influenza than among those with SARS-CoV-2 infection (11.4% vs 7.9%; P <.001). Influenza-associated ICU admission rates were 10.5% before the pandemic and 11.8% during the pandemic, while rates across SARS-CoV-2 periods ranged from 5.0% to 10.3%. The use of respiratory support was numerically greater with influenza, although the between-group difference did not reach statistical significance. Children with influenza also experienced significantly more complications (P <.001). The most common complication was lobar pneumonia and affected approximately 20% of children hospitalized with influenza during both influenza periods. Acute respiratory distress syndrome was reported only among patients with influenza and was not observed among those with SARS-CoV-2 infection. Antibiotics were administered to 40.7% of children with influenza compared with 14.4% of those with COVID-19 (P <.001). The most commonly administered antibiotics were amoxicillin-clavulanate, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. Several underlying conditions were independently associated with severe disease, defined as requiring invasive or noninvasive ventilation. Among children with SARS-CoV-2, these included cardiovascular conditions (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 6.37; 95% CI, 3.29-12.35), neurologic or neuromuscular conditions (aOR, 4.64; 95% CI, 2.52-8.51), and other underlying conditions (aOR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.05-3.55). For influenza, severe disease was associated with neurologic or neuromuscular conditions (aOR, 5.70; 95% CI, 3.07-10.59) and respiratory conditions (aOR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.04-4.98). Study limitations include an inability to determine whether infection was the primary reason for every hospitalization, changes in the number of participating hospitals over time, and the use of ventilation requirements to define severe disease. Vaccination data also were not systematically available. “Continued surveillance remains important to monitor changes in the clinical impact of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza in children and to inform vaccination and public health policy,” the researchers concluded. References: Zimmermann P, Sanchez C, Buettcher M, Heininger U, Bielicki JA, for the CH-SUR Study Group. OffOn Stream on FDA approves Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine Moderna was seeking approval for the vaccine's use in adults over 50. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Mary Kekatos, and Eric M. Strauss August 6, 2026, 3:59 AM The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. The vaccine, mFLUSIVA, is expected to be available for people 50 and older for the 2026-2027 respiratory illness season. "Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFLUSIVA provides an important new option for America's seniors. This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation," Stéphane Bancel, Chief Executive Officer of Moderna, said in a statement. In this Dec. 15, 2020, file photo, the Moderna, Inc. headquarters is shown in Cambridge, Mass. Elise Amendola/AP, FILE In a clinical trial for people aged 50 to 64, the mRNA vaccine led to 27% fewer confirmed flu cases than the current standard vaccine. The safety profile for Moderna’s vaccine and the current standard was about the same, but more people taking the mRNA vaccine reported side effects; those were mostly mild and lasted two days or less. For people 65 and older, a high-dose vaccine is currently recommended. Moderna said it will keep data this winter on how mFlusiva does compared to the current high-dose vaccine and submit that to the FDA to see if the vaccine remains approved for that population. Earlier this year, the FDA announced it would not review Moderna's application for the vaccine. However, the agency backtracked and agreed to review the shot after Moderna promised to conduct another study after the shot became available on the market. The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. Health UAE health ministry urges annual flu vaccination as seasonal influenza can lead to complications Ministry identifies six high-risk groups and says vaccination remains the most effective protection against seasonal influenza By Emad El-Din Khalil Published: 2026-09-21T08:25:00+04:00 3 min read The ministry stressed that annual vaccination and preventive measures remain the most effective way to reduce the impact of seasonal influenza and its complications. Dubai: The Ministry of Health and Prevention (MoHAP) has urged residents to receive the seasonal influenza vaccine, warning that the disease, which often begins with symptoms such as fever, cough, fatigue and muscle aches, can develop into a serious illness requiring hospitalisation, particularly among vulnerable groups. The ministry said influenza vaccination can provide up to 90 per cent protection against clinical illness in healthy adults and remains the most effective way to prevent infection, reduce the severity of illness and lower the risk of hospitalisation. Acute respiratory infection The ministry explained that seasonal influenza is an acute infectious respiratory disease caused by influenza viruses, which circulate during specific seasons, particularly in winter. Influenza viruses belong to the Orthomyxoviridae family and are classified into three types: A, B and C. MoHAP noted that the influenza vaccine is an inactivated vaccine containing virus particles that cannot cause the disease. The vaccine is available to everyone aged six months and above through government and private healthcare facilities across the UAE. Symptoms and transmission The ministry said seasonal influenza symptoms can range from mild to severe and generally resolve within a week without medical intervention. However, in some cases, the disease can lead to serious complications requiring hospitalisation. Symptoms include: Fever Headache Fatigue Cough Muscle aches Joint pain Sore throat Runny nose Vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly in children The incubation period is approximately two days and may range from one to four days. Influenza is transmitted through respiratory droplets released when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks. It can also spread indirectly through contact with contaminated hands, objects or surfaces, followed by touching the mouth, nose or eyes. Six high-risk groups The ministry identified six groups that are most vulnerable to influenza and its complications: Pregnant women at any stage of pregnancy Children under five years old Elderly people Healthcare workers Individuals with chronic medical conditions, including heart, lung, kidney, liver and blood diseases People with weakened or compromised immune systems MoHAP outlined seven key preventive measures: Receiving the influenza vaccine Following proper cough and sneeze etiquette Avoiding close contact with infected individuals Regularly cleaning and disinfecting frequently used surfaces and objects Washing and sanitising hands regularly Staying away from others when symptoms develop Avoiding touching the eyes, nose and mouth The ministry recommended receiving the vaccine annually in September or early winter before the start of the flu season. However, it stressed that vaccination remains beneficial even if received later, as influenza activity can continue for several months. It noted that the body requires approximately two weeks after vaccination to develop protection. Safe and effective vaccine The ministry emphasised that the influenza vaccine has been administered to millions of people worldwide for more than 60 years and has a strong safety record. According to the ministry, side effects are generally mild and resolve on their own within a few days. Global impact The ministry said seasonal influenza affects approximately 5 to 10 per cent of adults and 20 to 30 per cent of children worldwide each year. Globally, influenza results in an estimated three to five million severe cases annually and causes between 290,000 and 650,000 deaths from respiratory complications. While most people recover without complications, the ministry warned that the disease can lead to serious health consequences, particularly among high-risk groups. It also noted that every influenza season differs from the previous one and may affect people in different ways. Benefits of vaccination The ministry cited studies showing that influenza vaccination: Reduces the severity of illness in infected individuals Reduces hospital admissions among older adults by 25 to 39 per cent Reduces overall mortality by 39 to 75 per cent Provides approximately 70 to 90 per cent protection against clinical illness in healthy adults The ministry also highlighted five key benefits of vaccination: Protecting individuals from influenza infection Reducing the risk of hospitalisation Reducing the severity of illness Protecting pregnant women during and after pregnancy Protecting infants during their first months of life and contributing to community protection, particularly for vulnerable groups The ministry stressed that annual vaccination and preventive measures remain the most effective way to reduce the impact of seasonal influenza and its complications

"The seasonal flu vaccines are ordered by the Ministry of Health and we know that the order was made on time and in this regard, regarding the start of seasonal flu vaccination, there is no delay. On the contrary, this year we think that we will start earlier than last year and the population, especially those who are priority groups, will receive the vaccine on time, be immunized and be protected against seasonal flu", said Faik Hoti, a public health specialist. According to Hoti, the period in which seasonal flu circulates the most is a few weeks away. He said that vaccination in early autumn is the most appropriate time for immunization. "Usually, seasonal flu viruses are most active during November-December and usually reach their peak in January. However, in order to provide timely protection and to create immunity in at-risk groups, vaccination should begin earlier and we believe that starting vaccination in October represents an optimal opportunity and appropriate time to begin the process," said Hoti. Hoti said that 70,000 doses would be sufficient for interested citizens, but according to him, the Ministry of Health should always provide a larger number of vaccines. All citizens can receive the seasonal flu vaccine from the beginning of October until April 2027. According to the NIPHK, about 1 billion cases of seasonal influenza are reported each year worldwide, while up to 5 million cases occur in severe forms. Short Url https://arab.news/guw3p High-risk groups, including seniors, children, pregnant women, healthcare workers, advised to get vaccinated Updated 16 September 2026 Arab News Pakistan September 16, 2026 13:10 RIYADH: The Ministry of Health announced on Wednesday that it had started providing the seasonal influenza vaccine as part of efforts to promote preventive health and improve access to healthcare services. The ministry said groups most at risk of influenza complications included people with chronic diseases, those over 50, children aged six months to five years, pregnant women, people with severe obesity and healthcare workers, stressing the importance of vaccination. The ministry urged community members to book vaccination appointments through the Sehhaty app. It also offers home vaccination services through the Sanar app, focusing on vulnerable groups, including children, pregnant women and the elderly. According to the ministry, the vaccine reduces the severity of infections, the need for intensive care and influenza-related mortality. The ministry urged citizens and residents to take advantage of the services and get vaccinated, saying vaccination was a safe and effective way to prevent severe complications and reduce hospitalizations, particularly among high-risk groups. supplementary_news.content: Monday, September 21, 2026 / 10, Rabi al-thani, 1448 Since 1976 LEADING THE WAY Saudi Arabia World Business Opinion Sports Esports Lifestyle Video Discover Saudi Live Search Home >Saudi Arabia Health Ministry launches seasonal flu vaccine; urges high-risk groups to get shots September 16, 2026 | 04:55 PM The Ministry of Health revealed that 95.5 percent of influenza-related hospitalizations last year were those who failed to receive a vaccine. September 16, 2026 | 04:55 PM Saudi Gazette report Last Updated: September 16, 2026 | 04:55 PM 1 minute read AA Resize RIYADH — The Ministry of Health announced that it has started on Wednesday providing the seasonal influenza vaccine as part of its efforts to promote preventive health and facilitate access to healthcare services. The ministry noted that groups most at risk of complications from seasonal influenza include people with chronic diseases, those over 50, children aged six months to five years, pregnant women, people with severe obesity, and healthcare workers, stressing the importance of vaccination. The ministry revealed that 95.5 percent of influenza-related hospitalizations last year were those who failed to receive a vaccine. The ministry emphasized the vaccine's effectiveness in reducing the likelihood of contracting influenza and mitigating its complications. It noted that vaccination reduces the risk of death among the elderly by more than two-thirds. The ministry stressed the importance of annual vaccination, given the continuous changes in influenza virus strains, and urged all members of the society, especially those most vulnerable to complications, to get vaccinated. The ministry urged the public to book an appointment to receive the vaccine through the Sehhaty application. Dari 86 spesimen yang positif influenza, 76 merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09, menjadikannya subtipe yang paling banyak ditemukan. Meski meningkat, Kemenkes masih menilai aktivitas influenza di Indonesia berada dalam kategori rendah. This section summary was AI-assisted and reviewed by our editorial team. Share Article Aktivitas influenza di Indonesia menunjukkan peningkatan dalam beberapa pekan terakhir. Data terbaru Kementerian Kesehatan (Kemenkes) RI memperlihatkan A(H1N1)pdm09 menjadi subtipe influenza yang paling banyak ditemukan dalam pemeriksaan laboratorium. Dalam Laporan Pengawasan Kasus Influenza dan COVID-19 yang diperbarui pada 19 September 2026, Kemenkes mencatat proporsi spesimen positif influenza pada minggu ke-36 meningkat menjadi 46 persen, dari 35 persen pada minggu sebelumnya. Catatan penting: positivity rate 46 persen merupakan proporsi hasil positif di antara spesimen yang masuk ke sistem surveilans dan diperiksa. Table of Content 1. A(H1N1)pdm09 dominan 2. Pasien influenza yang dirawat di rumah sakit juga meningkat 3. Kasus paling banyak ditemukan pada anak kecil 4. Meski naik, tetapi aktivitas influenza masih dikategorikan rendah 5. Strain influenza yang dominan bisa berubah 1. A(H1N1)pdm09 dominan Pada minggu ke-36, sebanyak 185 spesimen diperiksa dan 86 di antaranya positif influenza. Dari kasus positif tersebut: 76 merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09 (88 persen) 8 merupakan A(H3N2) 2 merupakan influenza B/Victoria Dominasi serupa juga terlihat pada surveilans pelayanan kesehatan primer. Dari 122 spesimen yang diperiksa pada minggu ke-36, 60 positif influenza. Sebanyak 49 merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09, sementara empat A(H3), satu influenza B/Victoria, dan 6 belum ditentukan subtipenya. 2. Pasien influenza yang dirawat di rumah sakit juga meningkat Peningkatan juga terlihat pada jaringan rumah sakit sentinel. Kemenkes melaporkan bahwa proporsi kasus influenza positif di rumah sakit meningkat menjadi 31,7 persen dari 20,4 persen pada minggu sebelumnya. Dari 63 pasien yang dirawat dan diperiksa pada minggu ke-36, 20 positif influenza. Sebanyak 16 kasus merupakan A(H1N1)pdm09, tiga A(H3), dan satu influenza B/Victoria. Namun, tidak ada pasien influenza positif yang membutuhkan perawatan ICU pada minggu itu. 3. Kasus paling banyak ditemukan pada anak kecil ilustrasi influenza A (magnific.com/benzoix) Dalam data surveilans laboratorium, 42 persen kasus influenza yang terdeteksi berasal dari kelompok usia 0–4 tahun. Pada data rawat inap, Kemenkes juga mencatat kasus influenza paling banyak ditemukan pada kelompok usia 0–4 tahun. Anak kecil memang termasuk kelompok yang lebih mudah terkena influenza dan lebih berisiko mengalami komplikasi dibandingkan anak yang lebih besar atau orang dewasa sehat. Sistem imun mereka masih membangun pengalaman terhadap berbagai virus influenza, sementara lingkungan seperti daycare dan sekolah juga meningkatkan peluang paparan. 4. Meski naik, tetapi aktivitas influenza masih dikategorikan rendah Walaupun angka positivity rate meningkat, tetapi Kemenkes menyebut tingkat aktivitas influenza saat ini masih berada dalam kategori rendah dan masih sesuai dengan pola musiman influenza di Indonesia. Penilaian tersebut menggunakan indikator surveilans yang lebih luas, bukan cuma jumlah hasil positif dalam satu minggu. 5. Strain influenza yang dominan bisa berubah Virus influenza yang paling banyak beredar tidak selalu sama sepanjang tahun. Komposisi A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3), dan influenza B berubah-ubah sepanjang 2025–2026. Pada beberapa periode H3 lebih banyak ditemukan, sedangkan menjelang September 2026 proporsi H1N1pdm09 meningkat tajam. Perubahan seperti ini merupakan bagian dari pola epidemiologi influenza. Kekebalan masyarakat, karakter virus yang sedang beredar, musim, mobilitas, dan berbagai faktor lingkungan dapat ikut memengaruhi subtipe mana yang lebih banyak ditemukan pada suatu periode. Data terbaru mingguan Kemenkes ini menunjukkan bahwa aktivitas influenza sedang meningkat dan A(H1N1)pdm09 menjadi subtipe yang mendominasi, tetapi situasi secara keseluruhan masih berada dalam kategori aktivitas rendah. Tetap lindungi diri dengan menjaga kebersihan tangan, menerapkan etika batuk dan bersin, memakai masker ketika sakit, serta mendapatkan vaksin influenza tahunan, khususnya bagi kelompok rentan. I am Yukko, a pharmacist and childcare worker who is a mother of four. This year, the influenza season has started earlier than usual. In 2026, the start of the seasonal influenza season was announced on August 28th. This is reportedly the second earliest start since the current infectious disease surveillance system began in 1999. "It's still hot, but influenza is already here?" Many of you may be surprised by this. As the seasons progress into autumn and winter, children may have more opportunities to catch influenza. Therefore, this time, I will summarize the characteristics of influenza treatments often used for children, Oseltamivir, Xofluza, and Inavir from a pharmacist's perspective. *This article is based on public documents and package inserts as of September 2026. Please follow the instructions of your doctor or pharmacist regarding actual treatment. Are anti-influenza drugs always necessary? First, it is important to know that you do not always have to use anti-influenza drugs when you have influenza that. Anti-influenza drugs are expected to shorten the duration of fever by about 1 to 2 days if started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Doctors decide whether to use them by considering symptoms, age, and the risk of severe illness. Oseltamivir You might be more familiar with the name "Tamiflu." It is an oral medication, and it is basically used for 5 days for treatment. Dry syrup is sometimes used for children. Here, the "taste" of children's medicine is surprisingly important. Towa Pharmaceutical's Oseltamivir DS 3% "Towa" is designed with a banana flavor. It is also formulated to reduce the bitterness of the medicine, making it as easy as possible for children to take. On the other hand, side effects such as vomiting are known to occur with oseltamivir. If the child vomits after taking it, do not decide on your own to give them another dose; instead, inform your doctor or pharmacist about how long after taking the medicine the vomiting occurred and consult them. Xofluza A major feature of Xofluza is that treatment is basically completed with a single dose . It comes in tablets and granules, and the 2% granule packet is 10mg per packet. Also, the granules are strawberry flavored🍓. However, you may feel a bitter taste if it is kept in the mouth for a while. Oseltamivir is banana-flavored, and Xofluza granules are strawberry-flavored. Children's medicines are designed with various considerations for taste. Another feature of Xofluza is that the half-life of its active metabolite is long. On the other hand, side effects related to bleeding have been reported, and nosebleeds may occur. This does not mean that you will definitely have a nosebleed if you take it, but if you notice any concerning bleeding, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Also, because it is a single-dose medication, consult your doctor or pharmacist if the child vomits after taking it. The response will be determined based on the time and circumstances of the vomiting, but instead of taking Xofluza again, treatment with another anti-influenza drug, such as oseltamivir or Inavir, may be selected. Inavir Inavir is not an oral medication, but an inhalant. A key feature of this treatment is that it is used for only one day. However, with children, there is often the concern of, "Are they inhaling it properly?" At pharmacies and similar locations, practice devices are sometimes used to practice inhalation. There are also types that make a sound when inhaled with the necessary force, and the sound serves as a benchmark to confirm whether the child has the strength required for inhalation. Also, the irritation during inhalation can sometimes cause coughing or nausea. "They threw up after inhaling!" Even in such cases, since Inavir is an inhalant, you generally do not need to worry that "the medicine came out because they vomited," as you would with an oral medication. If you are worried or are unsure if the inhalation was successful, consult your doctor or pharmacist. And another thing to be aware of is lactose. Inavir uses lactose hydrate, and that lactose contains milk protein as an impurity. Therefore, caution is required if there is a history of hypersensitivity to dairy products. If you have ever had allergic symptoms from milk or dairy products, please inform your doctor or pharmacist when it is prescribed. Features of each of the 3 medications To summarize briefly: Oseltamivir → Oral medication. Used for 5 days. Banana-flavored products available. Watch for vomiting, etc. Xofluza → Oral medication. Finished in one dose. Granules are strawberry-flavored. Watch for bleeding. Inavir → Inhalant. Used for only one day. The key is whether they can inhale it. Also watch for hypersensitivity to dairy products. Rather than saying "which medicine is the best," whether the child can use it properly This perspective is also important. Be careful beyond just medication for the first two days With influenza, you also need to be aware of abnormal behavior in children. Abnormal behavior has been reported even when anti-influenza drugs are not used, and it has been observed regardless of the type of medication or whether it was taken. Therefore, a causal relationship between abnormal behavior and anti-influenza drugs has not been established. Since it often occurs within two days of the onset of fever, when a child has influenza, do not leave them alone for the first two days, regardless of whether they are taking medication or not. This is also a point to keep in mind. The taste of the medicine, the dosage form, how to take it, and whether it can be inhaled. When using medicine for children, these "little differences" are very important. "Will my child be able to take this medicine?" "Will they be able to inhale it?" "They threw it up, will they be okay?" In such cases, please consult your doctor or pharmacist. As a pharmacist, I hope to help reduce the burden on children and the family members caring for them, even if just a little. Thank you for reading until the end.😊 Yukko References ・Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Influenza (General Page)" ・Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare "Q&A on Comprehensive Measures for Acute Respiratory Infections (ARI) for Fiscal Year 2025" ・Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) "Xofluza Tablets 10mg / Xofluza Tablets 20mg / Xofluza Granules 2% Package Insert" ・Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) "Inavir Inhalation Powder 20mg Package Insert" ・Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) "Oseltamivir DS 3% 'Towa' Package Insert" ・Towa Pharmaceutical "Oseltamivir DS 3% 'Towa' Product Information" ・Shionogi & Co., Ltd. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, September 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology How Host Genes May Shape Influenza B Risk and Vaccine Response by Bioengineer September 21, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Influenza B virus has long lived in the shadow of its more notorious cousin, influenza A, yet it remains a substantial contributor to the seasonal burden of respiratory disease, particularly among children, adolescents, and older adults. A new review published in Virology Journal examines one of the least explored dimensions of this pathogen: the role of human immunogenetics in shaping who falls ill, how severely, and how well they respond to vaccination. The work, led by Ghayyas Ud Din and Hizbullah Khan, who share first authorship, alongside colleagues at institutions including the Shanghai Institute of Immunity and Infection and Guangdong Medical University, offers a careful stocktaking of what is known, what is merely inferred, and where the field must go next. Unlike influenza A, influenza B virus lacks a broad animal reservoir and, with it, the pandemic potential that makes influenza A a constant global security concern. But the absence of pandemic risk has never equated to clinical irrelevance. Influenza B virus drives substantial morbidity in seasonal epidemics, and its two historically circulating lineages, B/Victoria and B/Yamagata, have followed strikingly different trajectories in recent years. Surveillance has documented no confirmed naturally circulating B/Yamagata-lineage viruses since March 2020, a development widely linked to the intense non-pharmaceutical interventions of the COVID-19 pandemic era. Current influenza B activity is now overwhelmingly attributable to B/Victoria-lineage viruses, a shift with real consequences for vaccine composition and the interpretation of vaccine effectiveness studies. The central premise of the review is that the host genome may help explain a persistent puzzle: why individuals exposed to the same virus, and receiving the same vaccine, experience markedly different outcomes. Variation in genes governing antigen presentation, innate viral sensing, interferon signaling, and host dependency or restriction factors could plausibly generate heterogeneity in susceptibility, disease severity, cross-lineage immunity, and responsiveness to immunization. This framework draws on decades of immunogenetic research in influenza A and in broader antiviral biology, but the authors stress a crucial caveat: much of what has been proposed for influenza B rests on inference rather than on direct, influenza B virus-specific human data. Discover more genetic Biological Sciences genetics Parasites & Parasitic Diseases Infectious Diseases At the heart of the immunogenetic hypothesis lies the human leukocyte antigen system, the protein complex responsible for presenting viral peptide fragments to T cells. Differences in HLA alleles can alter which viral epitopes are displayed, how strongly T cells respond, and consequently how efficiently an infected or vaccinated individual clears virus or mounts protective memory. For influenza A, associations between specific HLA variants and outcomes such as infection risk, severity, and antibody titers after vaccination have been reported across multiple populations. Extending these findings to influenza B is not straightforward, however, because the two virus types differ in their evolutionary dynamics, transmission patterns, and the antigenic landscape they present to the immune system. Epitope repertoires are not interchangeable, and a genetic variant that enhances clearance of one influenza type may have little or no measurable effect on the other. Beyond antigen presentation, the review considers the innate immune machinery that first detects invading influenza viruses. Pattern recognition receptors such as the toll-like receptors and RIG-I-like receptors sense viral RNA and trigger signaling cascades that culminate in interferon production. Genetic polymorphisms in these sensors and in the downstream interferon pathway can modulate the vigor of the early antiviral response, potentially determining whether an infection is contained quickly or gains a foothold. Similarly, host dependency factors that the virus requires for entry, replication, and assembly, along with restriction factors that actively inhibit viral replication, represent additional layers where inherited variation could shape susceptibility. Each of these domains offers a plausible mechanistic route by which host genotype could influence influenza B outcomes, yet the authors find that direct evidence in the influenza B context remains sparse and fragmentary. When it comes to vaccine response, the review is similarly measured. The best-supported determinants of influenza vaccine performance, the authors conclude, are not genetic at all. Antigenic match between vaccine strains and circulating viruses, the continuous process of antigenic drift that erodes that match over time, the age of the vaccinee, prior exposure history, and baseline immunity stand out as the factors with the strongest evidentiary grounding. These non-genetic determinants have been repeatedly validated across seasons and populations, and they explain a considerable portion of the year-to-year variability in vaccine effectiveness. Genetic predictors specific to influenza B, by contrast, remain incompletely defined, and no validated host-genetic biomarker currently exists to guide vaccination decisions for this virus. This asymmetry between well-established extrinsic factors and poorly characterized intrinsic ones is not merely an academic gap. Predictive models of influenza B immune control and vaccine performance are limited by the absence of genotype-linked outcome data. Without large, well-phenotyped cohorts in which host genotype, immune phenotyping, and lineage-resolved virologic outcomes are collected together, the field cannot distinguish genuine genetic effects from confounding by age, prior exposure, or antigenic distance. The authors argue that such integrated studies represent the most important priority for future research, and they outline a research agenda built around linking these data streams in a single analytical framework. Discover more Genes genes Health Conditions Genetic Medical Literature & Resources The disappearance of the B/Yamagata lineage adds an unusual wrinkle to this agenda. With no naturally circulating Yamagata viruses detected for years, vaccine components targeting that lineage have become biologically obsolete, and regulatory and advisory bodies have been reconsidering the composition of seasonal vaccines, including the transition from quadrivalent to trivalent formulations. For immunogenetic studies, the loss of a circulating lineage complicates the interpretation of historical cross-lineage immunity data and underscores the need for lineage-resolved outcome measures in future cohorts. Any genetic association study conducted today will, in practice, be measuring responses against B/Victoria viruses, and generalizing those findings to influenza B as a whole carries inherent uncertainty. Population-specific variation presents another challenge. Immunogenetic associations identified in one ancestry or geographic setting frequently fail to replicate elsewhere, reflecting both genuine differences in allele frequencies and differences in study design, exposure patterns, and co-circulating pathogens. The international composition of the review team, spanning institutions in China, Pakistan, and Uzbekistan, reflects a growing recognition that influenza B research must extend beyond the settings where it has traditionally been studied. Building the evidence base for immunogenetic determinants will require multi-center collaborations with standardized genotyping platforms, harmonized immune phenotyping protocols, and consistent definitions of susceptibility, severity, and vaccine response. The review, which received support from the Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation and the Dongguan Science and Technology of Social Development Program, ultimately delivers a message of disciplined optimism. The biological logic connecting host genetic variation to influenza B outcomes is sound, and the methodological tools needed to test it, from affordable genome sequencing to sophisticated immune profiling, are now widely available. What is missing is the concerted, influenza B-specific data collection that would convert plausible mechanisms into clinically actionable knowledge. Until that work is done, antigenic match, age, and exposure history will remain the most reliable predictors of how influenza B behaves in populations, while the genome’s contribution waits to be quantified. Show original Out-of-season Influenza: The Difficulty of Answering 'When Can I Return to Work?' 1 ねりごま 2026年9月19日 08:57 Influenza has already entered a period of prevalence. At my workplace, we are busy responding to cases, such as diagnosing influenza A in outpatients and implementing infection control measures on one floor to curb the spread. This August onset is the second earliest since the Infectious Diseases Control Law was enacted in 1999. They say it's the second earliest, but do you know when the first was? It was 2009. It might be a story from long ago that many people don't know, but at the time it was called novel influenza. And this year, the virus said to be at the center of the outbreak is named A(H1N1)pdm09*. It is the same lineage as the virus that emerged in 2009. The WHO declared the end of the pandemic in August 2010, and since then, it has been treated as seasonal influenza. Seventeen years after its emergence in 2009, it continues to circulate every year as the same virus, while changing its appearance little by little. Even though it is the same virus, there is the 'novel' one that was considered a threat and the 'seasonal' one that is an annual occurrence. What separates the two? What separates them is 'the relationship between the virus and the immunity of the host'. The difference between novel and seasonal is not determined by the virus alone. It is determined by the relationship. In hospitals, too, there are events regarding influenza that are determined by relationships. Three things you receive at the hospital When diagnosed with influenza, you are given several things. Here, I will divide them into three: medication, documentation, and instructions on when you can return to school/work. I am on the side that hands these three things out. Those of us on the giving side actually think about what and how we should hand them over. Is it really necessary? How much should we explain? It is painful to listen to a long explanation when you are feverish and feeling sluggish, isn't it? "Medication" WHO guidelines do not target influenza treatment for healthy individuals without risks. In Western countries, the principle is to use nothing but antipyretics for healthy people, and even those are mainly for the purpose of relieving pain rather than for treatment. The US CDC also recommends antiviral drugs only for those at high risk of severe illness, such as the elderly or those with underlying conditions. Japan prescribes them widely, even to healthy adults and children. I want to go back to work quickly, I want the peace of mind that comes with getting medicine, other doctors have prescribed it for me. There is also the aspect that it is faster to prescribe than to carefully explain why you are not. It is not purely determined by medical reasons. Whether or not to prescribe medication is determined by the relationship with the patient. "Documentation" Medical certificates or certificates of recovery. In the Q&A issued by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, it is stated that submission of a certificate of recovery is unnecessary. It even goes so far as to say that it is undesirable for workplaces to require employees to submit certificates of recovery or negative test results. The same applies when returning to school. Workplaces also request them out of good intentions, saying, 'It wouldn't do to infect others.' --Those with less medical knowledge are institutionalizing based on worry. Patients request them because 'I can't work unless I submit it.' --In some cases, it becomes a significant expense out of pocket. Medical providers write them because 'I was asked to write one.' --Sometimes I ask, 'Wouldn't a receipt serve as proof of the visit?' Whether or not to issue documentation is determined not just by the body, but by the relationship with the workplace and living environment. To begin with, what constitutes a recovery? Is it the person's body, the shedding of the virus, or the risk of infecting others? I issue the standard form while harboring these vague feelings. "Instructions" For schools, there are standards under the School Health and Safety Act. The rules state that attendance is suspended until 5 days have passed since the onset and 2 days (3 days for infants) have passed since the fever subsided. This applies up to university level, so this applies to students even if they are adults. There is no uniform statutory number of days for returning to the workplace. Seasonal influenza is classified as a Category V infectious disease under the Infectious Diseases Control Law and is not subject to work restrictions. In other words, there is no legally mandated period for suspension from work. If your company has work regulations, you must follow them, but those are rules specific to each company. Incidentally, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare explains that since the virus is shed from the day before onset to 3–7 days after onset, one should refrain from going out while shedding the virus. This is not a rule divided by a specific number of days, and the way it is counted differs from school standards. Therefore, when asked 'When can I go back to work?', the basis for the answer changes depending on the person. For a student, it is based on legal requirements. For a working person, it depends on company rules and the individual's condition. I do explain it by saying something like, 'According to school attendance suspension standards...', though. 'I have opportunities to interact with elderly people; until when should I avoid seeing them?'... There is no absolute, clear-cut standard for that person. How long one must stay at home and alone is determined by one's relationships with those around them. The patient's perspective I believe the reasons for coming to the hospital also vary. Physical discomfort, fear of the illness becoming severe, not wanting to infect family members. And being told by a school or workplace to see a doctor. There is also the desire to be reassured by getting a clear diagnosis. Just knowing what the illness is can be a slight relief. Coming to the hospital for such different reasons, three things are returned for various reasons. All of that is determined by the relationship between the patient, the hospital, and society. Where do the reasons become invisible? On the side giving the information, different grounds are handled at once. Is it medicine, anxiety, legal requirements, or social circumstances? What is given is determined by the relationship with the situation you are in. But when it is received, it is all bundled together. When given together, it is easy for even the grounds to look the same. If you or your family are told at the hospital that it is influenza, I would like you to take a moment to re-examine the three things you were given. For what reason were they given? Medicine, society, or custom? What you received does not change. But I think the meaning of the explanation received looks a little different when you think about where the information came from, rather than just accepting it because 'it was given to you'. The virus that shocked the world 17 years ago is now called seasonal. The virus remains the same in its lineage; what has changed is the side receiving it. And the same thing is happening in the examination room. It is not just the name of the disease that determines what is given. ※A(H1N1)pdm09... An influenza virus that emerged in 2009 and caused a global pandemic. It currently circulates every year as one of the seasonal influenza strains. 投稿 ログイン 会員登録 SYSTEM NOTICE Auto translation by AI. Be sure, accuracy, nuances and authorial intent may not be fully reflected. Show original Influenza B arrives after the New Year. Does the vaccine given in September still work by then? ひろつ内科クリニック院長 / Dr.Hirotsu 2026年9月17日 10:58 “I heard that Influenza B becomes prevalent in the latter half of winter. Does the vaccine I received in September still work by then?” Since we started vaccinations, I have begun to receive questions like this. I think it is a good question. And, to answer honestly, there is no clean answer. I will write three things first. It is true according to data that the detection of Influenza B has been skewed toward the period after the New Year for the past several seasons. However, whether the effect of a vaccine given in September lasts until that time has not been settled yet. And, I do not make the decision to delay vaccination based on the fact that it is not settled. It is true that Influenza B is skewed toward the latter part of the season Looking at the weekly detection reports from the National Institute of Health Crisis Management, of the 3,962 cases of Influenza B detected last season (2025/26), 94.7% were after the New Year. 90.4% occurred in January to March alone. The peaks were also 13 weeks apart, with A(H3) in the 47th week of 2025 and B/Victoria in the 7th week of 2026. The same pattern appeared in 2023/24 and 2024/25. However, when it comes and how much of it comes are different things. The proportion of Influenza B in the entire season fluctuates from 2.3% to 45.0% depending on the year. In 2022/23, it was 2.3%, with only 91 cases. There are years when it comes and years when it hardly comes at all. The premise has also changed. The B/Yamagata lineage has not been detected in Japan for six consecutive seasons since 2020/21. Japanese vaccines have also become trivalent since 2025/26, so now when we say “Influenza B,” we mean B/Victoria. The point is not whether to get two doses The dosage in the package insert is one dose for those 13 and older, or two doses at an interval of about 1 to 4 weeks. The two-dose vaccination described is for this interval, and a method of getting one dose in September and another several months later is not written. As far as I have confirmed, there are no public institutions that recommend additional vaccinations for adults during the season. Therefore, the point is not whether to get two doses. It is how long the effect of one dose lasts. I would not recommend that those who were vaccinated in September get vaccinated again for the latter half of winter. I think it is fine to consider that as completed. That “how long” has not been settled There is a 2025 report that analyzed the time after 5 months from vaccination in healthy adults aged 18 to 65. I will write how to read the numbers first. The following is an indicator (adjusted odds ratio) showing that the lower the value is below 1, the fewer infections there were among vaccinated people, and if the range shown together (95% confidence interval) straddles 1, it means “it could not be determined whether there was a difference or not.” A(H1N1)pdm09 was 0.66, with a range of 0.51 to 0.87. It does not straddle 1. It is a value that can be read as protection remaining. On the other hand, Influenza B was 0.75, with a range of 0.49 to 1.16. It straddles 1. Even though the value itself points toward protection, it cannot be stated definitively. This is a point that is easily misunderstood. “Not significant” does not mean “no effect.” It means it could not be determined within the scope of this analysis. For the same reason, there is no basis to say definitively that “Influenza B will also last without problems.” The research itself is divided There are reports that detected a decline and reports that found no evidence, both exist. On the side of a decline, a 2016 report showed effectiveness against Influenza B was 70.7% (51.3–82.4) 44 days after vaccination, and 21.4% (−57.4–60.8) at the end of the season. However, since the range at the end of the season straddles 0, it cannot be read as “it dropped to 21%.” In a 2018 report, the amount of change for Influenza B was −19 (−33 to −6). On the side of no decline, an analysis of a total of 210,000 cases in the UK stated that “there was evidence of a decline for Influenza A, but no evidence of a decline for Influenza B.” A 2025 report looking at hospitalizations in the US showed Influenza B at 67% (35–84), which was higher than the 36% (21–48) for A(H1N1). A 2026 review summarizing 49 studies states that attenuation was observed more consistently for Influenza A, especially A(H3N2), than for Influenza B. In short, neither the claim that "Type B protection wanes quickly" nor "Type B protection does not wane" can be supported by the current evidence. Not only is the magnitude of the conclusion unclear, but the findings are not even consistent in direction. To be clear, the reason this remains unresolved is only a matter of how much protection against Type B remains in the latter half of winter. It does not mean that getting vaccinated in September was a waste, and the protection against the currently circulating Type A has been working since the moment you received the shot. I will leave what is unknown as it is. It has not been determined whether the observed decline is truly a waning of immunity or a bias stemming from research methodology. Many of the studies cited here include periods when the B/Yamagata lineage was still circulating. There is no data available that looks specifically at B/Victoria by days elapsed since vaccination. There is no data in Japan on Type B stratified by days elapsed since vaccination. All of it comes from overseas reports, and we are applying that to the situation in Japan. None of the reports cited so far are randomized controlled trials that directly verified whether the results for Type B change between September and November vaccinations. We do not even know if Type B will arrive this season. Domestic detections this season (weeks 32-36) include 56 cases of A(H1N1)pdm09, 1 case of A(H3), and 0 cases of Type B. Since there is no prediction that can provide a probability, I will not write down any numbers. Even so, I will not delay it. In Japan, the guideline for seasonal influenza vaccination is to start from mid-to-late October and finish by early December. Our clinic began vaccinations on September 12th to accommodate those who wish to be vaccinated at this time, and this does not replace the guidelines. Furthermore, regarding the question of "Why not wait until November?": A 2020 modeling study estimated that if vaccinations were delayed until October, more than 14% of those who had previously been vaccinated in August or September would miss their chance, potentially leading to an increase in hospitalizations. The decision to delay is conditional on the assumption that those who delay will actually come back to get vaccinated; if the rate of missed vaccinations exceeds a certain level, it could result in a net loss. This is based on a US modeling study, not a Japanese estimate. I will provide overseas recommendations as supplementary information. They do not replace Japanese recommendations. The US Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices does not recommend vaccination in July and August, but considers September and October to be ideal times. Canada's recommendations for this season also state that early autumn vaccination provides protection for the majority of the season. What is currently being detected is A(H1N1)pdm09. As mentioned in the previous review, waning is more consistently observed with Type A, so this does not mean there is no need to worry about Type A. Even so, I do not delay preparations for an ongoing outbreak based on the unresolved status of Type B. What you can do now for the latter half of winter If you develop a fever after the New Year, please consult us rather than deciding for yourself that it is not influenza because you were vaccinated. Having the whole family vaccinated is one approach. A randomized controlled trial involving a community overseas reported that vaccinating children indirectly reduced infections among unvaccinated people around them. While it has not been confirmed that the same result will occur in a household, it is one way of thinking about it. Hand washing and ventilation should be continued through the latter half of winter. I realize that writing that something is unknown when it is unknown makes for an unsatisfying article. Nevertheless, since there is not enough evidence to write about this definitively, I will leave it as it is. Reference: National Institute of Health Crisis Management "Weekly Influenza Virus Isolation/Detection Report" / "Infectious Diseases Weekly Report 2026 Week 36" / Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Press Release, 2026/27 Season Seasonal Influenza Vaccine Materials / Influenza HA Vaccine Package Insert / Nazareth J, et al. Lancet Microbe 2025;6(11):101136 / Kissling E, et al. Euro Surveill 2016;21(16):30201 / Young B, et al. J Infect Dis 2018;217(5):731-741 / Whitaker HJ, et al. Influenza Other Respir Viruses 2025;19(12):e70194 / Lewis NM, et al. J Infect Dis 2025;232(4):e626-e636 / Doyon-Plourde P, et al. CCDR 2026;52(6):231-245 / Ferdinands JM, et al. Clin Infect Dis 2020;70(8):1550-1559 / Grohskopf LA, et al. MMWR 2025;74(32):500-507 / Loeb M, et al. JAMA 2010;303(10):943-950 Our clinic has been providing influenza vaccinations since September 12th. We also support municipal public funding (routine vaccination) for those aged 65 and over, and the out-of-pocket cost and conditions depend on municipal regulations. For those not eligible for public funding, voluntary vaccination (at your own expense) is 4,000 yen per dose (tax included, including consultation fee).
